## Small box, big ideas

In the last section we stated that a container provides a reproducible
computing environment for a software application. How exactly do they do that?

It is helpful to start at the beginning of a container lifecycle.
Suppose a developer wants to make their
application available as a container, a role you will take on in
[Module 2: Building Containers](../02-building-and-publishing/index.qmd). They write
installation steps, such as 'download an external library' or 'compile
application code', in a text file called a `Containerfile` (`Dockerfile` if
you use Docker). A tool such as Podman reads these instructions and builds an
*image*.

You can think of an image as a read-only software disc. Internally, an image is
made up of a stack of *layers* rather than a single file,
but for our purposes it is enough to consider it to be an immutable, compact format.
It holds an application's code as well as everything that application needs to run, because the
dependencies were included during the build. This means it can be shared and
run directly on different computers *without* any installation steps:
a new user simply *pulls* (downloads) the image from a *registry*, which
acts as an online software library for
images, and a container *runtime* such as Podman runs it. Each running instance
of an image is one *container*.

The runtime reads the image and launches the application in a new environment,
which is mostly isolated from the rest of your system. The container has its
own filesystem, and by default its processes cannot see processes outside it.
In practice, you often want to share things with the application, such as
data files and network ports, or run extra commands inside it. The runtime
provides the interface between the containerised application and your system.

![Schematic for the lifecycle of containerised softare, from the left: a
Containerfile defines an image that is published to an online registry (cloud).
The image may be downloaded (disc) and used to run a sandboxed instance of 
the application (box).](assets/container-schematic.png)

## Containers and virtual machines

For those of you who have some experience with research computing, containers
may remind you of virtual machines. Both provide environment isolation but
to different extents.  A virtual machine encapsulates an
entire computer, including performing a full boot of an operating system. A container
instead uses a kernel&mdash;the core system program that manages hardware and processes&mdash;provided
by the host (e.g., your laptop), and isolates only an application's processes
and filesystem. Containers are therefore a higher level of virtualisation.

The main advantage of the level of virtualisation provided by containers is that they are more
resource efficient than virtual machines. Since there is no operating system to
boot, containerised applications start up almost immediately and add little
overhead to running the application outside the container. A trade-off is
weaker isolation, because the operating system's kernel is shared, which
has implications for security. It also means differences in host kernels
can potentially affect the reproducibility of the software (e.g., a kernel bug).

This is why containers are sometimes called *sandboxes*: they are a separate,
controlled space for an application to run, but the sandbox has weaker
isolation than a complete virtual machine.

::: {.callout-note collapse=true}
## Linux containers on Windows and macOS

On Linux, containers run using the host kernel, but this is not 
true for Windows and macOS. On those systems, a Linux virtual machine is created
by Podman (this is the *Podman machine* that was created during [installation](../00-prerequisites/index.qmd)),
and all containers run inside this. So containers on Windows and macOS in fact
involve both kinds of virtualisation!
:::

## Putting it all together

A **container** is an isolated, running instance of an application together with
its environment. The key terms are:

- **Containerfile:** a text file of build instructions
- **Image:** an immutable package, built from a Containerfile, containing the
  application and its dependencies
- **Registry:** an online store from which images are published and pulled
- **Container runtime:** the software, such as Podman, that runs images as
  containers

A user needs only a container runtime in order to run an image in a container.
Since runtimes such as Podman can be installed on every major operating
system, this makes containerised software highly accessible. For this
reason  containers have become a widely adopted mode of distributing software.
Barriers around installation are removed, and the repeatable, sandboxed environment
of a container, in which the versions of the application and its dependencies are
fixed, supports reproducibility.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Check your understanding

1. If you run the same container image twice, how many containers are created?
2. Explain how a virtual machine differs from a container.
3. What is a container registry?

:::

::: {.callout-note collapse=true}
## Answers

1. Two&mdash;each container is a separate running instance of the image.
2. A virtual machine boots its own operating system, whereas a container
   isolates only an application's processes and filesystem. Containers on the
   same host share a kernel.
3. A registry is an online service for storing and distributing container
   images.
:::
